notes:
1. NITI Aayog — Background and Need

  • India's economic structure changed significantly after the 1991 reforms.
  • Markets, private investment, technology, global integration and State Governments became more important in development.
  • The earlier highly centralised planning model became less suitable for this changed environment.
  • A new institution was needed for flexible policymaking, greater State participation, strategic guidance, monitoring, evaluation and innovation.

2. NITI Aayog — Establishment

  • NITI Aayog was established with effect from 1 January 2015.
  • It replaced the Planning Commission.
  • The 1950 resolution establishing the Planning Commission was superseded.
📌 Must-Memorise

NITI Aayog → 1 January 2015

3. NITI — Full Form

NITI stands for:

National Institution for Transforming India

📌 Must-Memorise

NITI → National Institution for Transforming India

4. Constitutional and Legal Status

  • NITI Aayog was constituted through a resolution of the Union Cabinet.
  • It was not created directly by the Constitution.
  • It was not established by an Act of Parliament.
  • It is therefore non-constitutional and non-statutory.
📌 Must-Memorise

NITI Aayog → Executive + Non-Constitutional + Non-Statutory

⚠️ TNPSC Trap

NITI Aayog ≠ Constitutional Body

NITI Aayog ≠ Statutory Body

5. NITI Aayog — Institutional Character

  • NITI Aayog functions as the Government of India's apex policy think tank.
  • It provides strategic, directional and technical policy inputs.
  • Its role differs from the old centralised resource-allocation model of the Planning Commission.
📌 Must-Memorise

NITI Aayog → Apex Policy Think Tank

6. Policy Advice — Union, States and Union Territories

NITI Aayog provides policy inputs to:

  • Union Government.
  • State Governments.
  • Union Territories.

Its purpose is to improve coordination and strengthen policy design across levels of government.

7. Core Philosophy — States as Development Partners

  • NITI Aayog treats States as active partners in development.
  • National development is expected to emerge through partnership between the Union and the States.
  • States are not viewed merely as recipients of centrally designed Plans.

8. Cooperative Federalism

  • Continuous promotion of cooperative federalism is one of NITI Aayog's central objectives.
  • It seeks greater consultation and partnership between the Union and State Governments.
📌 Must-Memorise

NITI Aayog → Cooperative Federalism

9. Strong States — Strong Nation

  • NITI Aayog's philosophy considers strong States essential for building a strong nation.
  • State development is therefore treated as an integral part of national development.
📌 Memory Chain

Strong States → Strong Nation → Cooperative Federalism

10. Bottom-Up Planning

  • NITI Aayog encourages planning from lower levels of government upward.
  • It seeks to reduce dependence on development planning designed entirely at the national level.
  • Local needs are intended to influence higher-level priorities.
📌 Must-Memorise

NITI Aayog → Bottom-Up Planning

11. Bottom-Up Planning — Local to National Chain

  • Village-level planning identifies local development requirements.
  • Local Plans can be progressively aggregated at higher levels.
📌 Must-Memorise

Village → District → State → National

12. Strategic and Long-Term Policy Role

  • NITI Aayog formulates strategic and long-term policy and programme frameworks.
  • It looks beyond immediate administrative needs towards future development challenges.
  • Policy work can cover agriculture, industry, infrastructure, energy, health, education, employment, skills, technology, urbanisation and environment.

13. Programme Monitoring and Mid-Course Correction

  • NITI Aayog monitors the progress and effectiveness of government programmes.
  • Monitoring feedback can be used to improve implementation while a programme is still underway.
  • This process supports mid-course correction.
📌 Must-Memorise

Monitoring → Feedback → Mid-Course Correction

14. Vulnerable Sections — Inclusive Development

  • NITI Aayog seeks to give special attention to sections of society that may not adequately benefit from economic progress.
  • Inclusion is therefore an important part of its development approach.

15. Innovation, Entrepreneurship and Technology

NITI Aayog promotes:

  • Innovation.
  • Entrepreneurship.
  • Technology adoption.
  • New development solutions.
  • Technology is treated as a tool for improving productivity, governance and development outcomes.

16. Capacity Building

  • NITI Aayog promotes capacity building in government and development institutions.
  • Better administrative capability is considered important for effective policy implementation.

17. Inter-Sectoral and Inter-Departmental Coordination

  • NITI Aayog provides a platform for resolving problems involving multiple sectors.
  • It can also help address issues involving several government departments.
  • This is important because development problems often cut across administrative boundaries.

18. Research and Knowledge Partnerships

NITI Aayog collaborates with:

  • Research institutions.
  • Experts.
  • Practitioners.
  • National think tanks.
  • International think tanks.
  • These partnerships support evidence-based policymaking.

19. Chairperson — Prime Minister

  • The Prime Minister of India serves as the Chairperson of NITI Aayog.
📌 Must-Memorise

NITI Aayog Chairperson → Prime Minister

20. Vice-Chairperson

  • NITI Aayog provides for a Vice-Chairperson.
  • The Vice-Chairperson is appointed by the Prime Minister.
📌 Must-Memorise

Vice-Chairperson → Appointed by Prime Minister

21. Members — Organisational Structure

The institutional framework provides for:

  • Full-time members.
  • Part-time members.
  • Ex officio members.
  • Special invitees where required.
  • Union Ministers may serve as ex officio members.

22. Chief Executive Officer — CEO

  • NITI Aayog has a Chief Executive Officer.
  • The CEO is appointed by the Prime Minister.
  • The CEO performs an important administrative and executive role.
📌 Must-Memorise

NITI Aayog CEO → Appointed by Prime Minister

23. Secretariat

  • A Secretariat supports NITI Aayog's policy, research, administrative and coordination functions.

24. Governing Council — Federal Platform

  • The Governing Council is the principal federal-level platform of NITI Aayog.
  • It helps develop shared national development priorities.
📌 Must-Memorise

Governing Council → Main Federal Platform

25. Governing Council — Composition

The framework includes:

  • Prime Minister as head.
  • Chief Ministers of States.
  • Elected leadership of Union Territories with legislatures.
  • Lieutenant Governors or Administrators of other Union Territories.
  • Vice-Chairperson and members.
  • Special invitees where required.

26. Governing Council — Main Functions

The Governing Council discusses:

  • National development priorities.
  • Major policy strategies.
  • Implementation issues.
  • Inter-State concerns.
  • Inter-sectoral issues.
  • State-specific development problems.
📌 Must-Memorise

Governing Council → Cooperative Federalism in Practice

27. Regional Councils

  • NITI Aayog's institutional framework provides for Regional Councils.
  • They may be constituted for a specified period to address issues affecting more than one State or a particular region.

Membership may include:

  • Chief Ministers.
  • Lieutenant Governors.
  • Relevant representatives.

28. Regional Councils — Possible Issues

Regional Councils can help address:

  • River-basin management.
  • Infrastructure connectivity.
  • Environmental concerns.
  • Agricultural problems.
  • Other inter-State development issues.

29. Cooperative Federalism — Meaning

  • Cooperative federalism means different levels of government work together to achieve common development objectives.
  • It encourages active participation of States in shaping national priorities.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Cooperative Federalism ≠ Elimination of Constitutional Division of Powers

30. Competitive Federalism

  • Competitive federalism encourages States and Union Territories to improve their performance through comparison and competition.
  • Rankings and indicators can reveal development gaps and identify better-performing policies.
📌 Must-Memorise

Competitive Federalism → Comparison + Competition + Better Performance

31. Cooperative vs Competitive Federalism

  • Cooperative Federalism → Governments work together.
  • Competitive Federalism → Governments improve through performance comparison.
📌 Must-Memorise

Cooperate → Work Together

Compete → Perform Better

32. NITI Aayog Uses Both Federal Approaches

  • Cooperative and competitive federalism are complementary.
  • NITI Aayog promotes both collaboration and performance-based comparison.

33. Rankings and Performance Indicators

NITI Aayog uses:

  • Rankings.
  • Indices.
  • Development indicators.
  • Comparative performance data.

These can help:

  • Identify weak outcomes.
  • Compare States and districts.
  • Detect successful policies.
  • Share best practices.

34. State-Specific and Local Solutions

  • Development needs differ across villages, districts, States and regions.
  • A policy suitable for one State may not be suitable for another.
  • NITI Aayog therefore emphasises local and State-specific development solutions.

35. Monitoring — Meaning

  • Monitoring examines whether a programme is progressing according to its objectives.
📌 Must-Memorise

Monitoring → Is the Programme Progressing?

36. Evaluation — Meaning

  • Evaluation examines whether a programme is producing intended results and using public resources effectively.
📌 Must-Memorise

Evaluation → Is the Programme Producing Results?

37. Monitoring vs Evaluation

  • Monitoring → Tracks ongoing progress.
  • Evaluation → Assesses effectiveness and outcomes.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Monitoring ≠ Evaluation

38. Development Monitoring and Evaluation Office — DMEO

  • DMEO stands for Development Monitoring and Evaluation Office.
  • It supports NITI Aayog's monitoring and evaluation functions.
  • It functions as an attached office associated with NITI Aayog.
📌 Must-Memorise

DMEO → Development Monitoring and Evaluation Office

39. DMEO — Main Assessment Areas

Evaluation can examine:

  • Programme effectiveness.
  • Efficiency of public-resource use.
  • Development outcomes.
  • Service delivery.
  • Programme impact.

40. Inputs to Outcomes — Governance Shift

  • Traditional assessment often focused heavily on expenditure and allocation.
  • NITI Aayog's monitoring framework reflects a broader shift towards results and outcomes.
📌 Must-Memorise

Old Focus → Inputs / Allocation

New Focus → Outcomes / Results

41. Sustainable Development Goals — SDGs

  • SDGs are global development goals under the United Nations 2030 Agenda.
  • NITI Aayog plays a central institutional role in advancing and monitoring them in India.
📌 Must-Memorise

SDG Monitoring in India → NITI Aayog

42. SDGs and Federalism

  • NITI Aayog works with States and Union Territories in advancing SDG implementation.
  • SDG comparisons also support competitive federalism.

43. SDG India Index and Dashboard

  • NITI Aayog developed the SDG India Index and Dashboard.
  • It compares the progress of States and Union Territories towards the Sustainable Development Goals.
📌 Must-Memorise

SDG India Index → State + UT Performance

44. First SDG India Index — December 2018

  • The first SDG India Index was launched in December 2018.
📌 Must-Memorise

First SDG India Index → December 2018

45. SDG India Index — Development Use

The Index helps:

  • Compare social performance.
  • Compare economic performance.
  • Compare environmental outcomes.
  • Identify development gaps.
  • Encourage governments to improve results.
📌 Must-Memorise

SDG India Index → Competitive Federalism Tool

46. Aspirational Districts Programme — January 2018

  • The Aspirational Districts Programme was launched in January 2018.
  • It focuses on 112 developmentally challenged districts.
📌 Must-Memorise

Aspirational Districts Programme → January 2018

Districts → 112

47. Aspirational Districts — Core Approach

The programme follows:

  • Convergence.
  • Collaboration.
  • Competition.
📌 Must-Memorise

Aspirational Districts → Convergence + Collaboration + Competition

48. Aspirational Districts — Major Development Areas

Performance is monitored in areas such as:

  • Health and nutrition.
  • Education.
  • Agriculture and water resources.
  • Financial inclusion.
  • Skill development.
  • Basic infrastructure.

49. Aspirational Districts — Data-Driven Governance

  • The programme uses measurable indicators and comparative rankings.
  • It is an important example of data-driven development administration.
  • Districts are encouraged to improve performance through continuous comparison.

50. Aspirational Blocks Programme

  • NITI Aayog's development framework also includes the Aspirational Blocks Programme.
  • It extends a similar results-oriented approach to selected blocks.
  • The move from districts to blocks reflects deeper local-level targeting of development gaps.

51. NITI Aayog — Knowledge Institution

  • NITI Aayog functions as a knowledge and policy-research institution.
  • It publishes policy papers, research papers, working papers and development reports.

52. Atal Innovation Mission

  • Atal Innovation Mission is associated with promotion of innovation and entrepreneurship.
  • It forms part of the broader effort to develop an innovation ecosystem.
📌 Must-Memorise

Atal Innovation Mission → Innovation + Entrepreneurship

53. Development Administration — NITI Aayog Role

NITI Aayog contributes through:

  • Policy design.
  • Coordination.
  • Monitoring.
  • Evaluation.
  • Data use.
  • Innovation.
  • Best-practice sharing.

54. Development Administration — Multi-Sector Coordination

Development areas often require coordination across several institutions.

Examples:

  • Health and nutrition → Multiple departments and levels of government.
  • Education → Union, State and local institutions.
  • Agriculture → Irrigation, credit, technology and markets.
  • Infrastructure → Inter-sectoral and inter-governmental coordination.
  • Skill development → Education, industry and labour-market coordination.

55. Policy Feedback and Redesign

  • Implementation experience is used to improve policies.
  • Weak outcomes identified through monitoring can lead to redesign.
  • Evaluation findings can improve administrative processes.
  • Better data can improve targeting and programme implementation.

56. Planning Commission vs NITI Aayog — Establishment and Status

  • Planning Commission → 1950.
  • NITI Aayog → 2015.
  • Both were created through executive action.
  • Both are non-constitutional and non-statutory institutions.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Planning Commission and NITI Aayog → Both Non-Constitutional

57. Five-Year Plan Role — Major Difference

  • Planning Commission was closely associated with preparation of Five-Year Plans.
  • NITI Aayog does not prepare traditional Five-Year Plans.
📌 Must-Memorise

Five-Year Plans → Planning Commission

NITI Aayog → No Traditional Five-Year Plan Role

58. Resource Allocation — Major Difference

  • Planning Commission historically played an important role in determining State Plan sizes and Plan assistance.
  • NITI Aayog primarily functions as a policy advisory, coordination, monitoring and knowledge institution.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

NITI Aayog ≠ Traditional Plan-Fund Allocation Authority

59. Top-Down vs Bottom-Up Approach

  • Planning Commission → More top-down orientation.
  • NITI Aayog → Greater bottom-up orientation.
📌 Must-Memorise

Planning Commission → Top-Down

NITI Aayog → Bottom-Up

60. Centralised vs Cooperative Orientation

  • Planning Commission operated within a relatively centralised planning framework.
  • NITI Aayog emphasises partnership between Union and States.
📌 Must-Memorise

Planning Commission → Centralised

NITI Aayog → Cooperative Federalism

61. Directive vs Market-Oriented Environment

  • Planning Commission developed in an era of stronger government control over investment and production.
  • NITI Aayog was designed for an economy in which markets, private investment, States, technology and global integration play much larger roles.

62. Planning Commission vs NITI Aayog — Core Difference

Planning Commission:

  • Central planning.
  • Five-Year Plans.
  • Plan-resource allocation.
  • More top-down.

NITI Aayog:

  • Strategic policy advice.
  • Federal coordination.
  • Monitoring and evaluation.
  • Greater State participation.
  • More bottom-up.
  • Greater emphasis on outcomes.

63. NITI Aayog — Core Institutional Identity

NITI Aayog =

2015

  • Executive Resolution
  • Non-Constitutional
  • Non-Statutory
  • Policy Think Tank
  • Cooperative Federalism
📌 Must-Memorise

This is the core identity chain.

64. Federalism Memory Chain

  • Cooperative Federalism → Work together.
  • Competitive Federalism → Perform better.
  • Governing Council → Federal platform.
  • Bottom-Up Planning → Local to national.

65. Monitoring Memory Chain

  • Monitoring → Track progress.
  • Evaluation → Assess results.
  • DMEO → Monitoring + Evaluation.
  • Feedback → Mid-course correction.

66. SDG Memory Chain

  • SDGs → UN 2030 Agenda.
  • NITI Aayog → Nodal institution in India.
  • SDG India Index → State and UT comparison.
  • First Index → December 2018.

67. Aspirational Districts Memory Chain

  • Launch → January 2018.
  • Districts → 112.
  • Approach → Convergence + Collaboration + Competition.
  • Method → Data + Indicators + Rankings.

68. Major Functions — Memory Chain

NITI Aayog functions include:

  • Strategic policy advice.
  • Long-term planning.
  • Cooperative federalism.
  • Competitive federalism.
  • State participation.
  • Bottom-up planning.
  • Monitoring.
  • Evaluation.
  • Innovation.
  • Research.
  • Knowledge sharing.
  • Capacity building.

69. High-Yield Chronology

  • 1950 → Planning Commission established.
  • 1991 → Economic reforms increased the role of markets and private investment.
  • 1 January 2015 → NITI Aayog established.
  • January 2018 → Aspirational Districts Programme launched.
  • December 2018 → First SDG India Index launched.

70. TNPSC Traps

  • NITI Aayog was established in 2015, not 2014.
  • Exact effective date → 1 January 2015.
  • NITI stands for National Institution for Transforming India.
  • NITI Aayog was created through executive action.
  • It is non-constitutional.
  • It is non-statutory.
  • Prime Minister is Chairperson.
  • Vice-Chairperson is appointed by the Prime Minister.
  • CEO is appointed by the Prime Minister.
  • NITI Aayog functions as an apex policy think tank.
  • It does not operate as the old central Five-Year Plan authority.
  • It does not perform the Planning Commission's traditional Plan-fund allocation role.
  • Governing Council is a major mechanism of cooperative federalism.
  • Chief Ministers participate in the Governing Council.
  • Regional Councils can address issues affecting more than one State.
  • Cooperative federalism means Union and States work together.
  • Competitive federalism means performance improves through comparison.
  • Cooperative and competitive federalism are complementary.
  • Bottom-up planning begins at lower levels of government.
  • Monitoring and evaluation are different.
  • DMEO stands for Development Monitoring and Evaluation Office.
  • NITI Aayog plays a central role in SDG monitoring in India.
  • SDG India Index compares States and Union Territories.
  • First SDG India Index → December 2018.
  • Aspirational Districts Programme → January 2018.
  • Aspirational Districts → 112.
  • Core Aspirational District approach → Convergence + Collaboration + Competition.
  • Atal Innovation Mission → Innovation and entrepreneurship.
  • Planning Commission and NITI Aayog are both non-constitutional institutions.
  • Planning Commission was more centralised.
  • NITI Aayog emphasises strategic advice and federal partnership.
  • Planning Commission had a stronger resource-allocation role.
  • NITI Aayog gives greater emphasis to monitoring, outcomes and policy feedback.
  • Replacement of Planning Commission did not mean development policymaking ended.

  • SDG Monitoring → NITI Aayog.
